newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: GOVERNMENT AGAIN RULES OUT APOLOGY TO STOLEN CHILDREN
The Federal Government has again ruled out an apology to the Stolen Generation, saying it won't seek further legal advice on the matter.
The Prime Minister has said there are significant legal implications for compensation claims if the Government formally apologises.
But Chief General Counsel, Henry Burmester, has told a Senate hearing original advice to Mr Howard had been sought in hurry and it may be possible to draft an apology which wouldn't incur liability.
The Acting Federal Attorney-General, Philip Ruddock has told ABC Radio Mr Burmester also made it clear it may NOT be possible to draft an apology that wouldn't give rise to compensation claims.
Mr Ruddock says the Government will make a considered response, but has made its position clear.
STRONG PICK UP IN HOUSING INDUSTRY
The number of homes financed in April rose by more than 12% on the previous month.
The Bureau of Statistics says seasonally adjusted, 43,600 dwellings were financed in April, the highest level recorded since July 1994.
The strong pick-up in housing follows two months of falls.
The rising confidence is probably related in part to the delayed impact of mortgage interest rate cuts late last year.
Analysts expect the latest interest rate cut late last month to further buoy future investment in housing.
CALL FOR FAMILY-FRIENDLY WORKPLACES
The Prime Minister's adviser on women's affairs says those lobbying for more flexible work conditions should focus on the productivity benefits to employers.
Pru Goward, who heads the Office of the Status of Women, says employers are likely to sack workers demanding new conditions as rights, unless the business benefits are made clear to them.
Ms Goward has told a Sydney conference on work and the family, there's nothing wrong with arguing that women and children deserve certain things.

But she says employers who have to meet the bottom line every week, are understandably less interested in that, than they are in their own fortunes and the survivability of themselves and their employees.
Ms Goward says a new approach is needed to achieve family-friendly workplaces.
CASE AGAINST JABILUKA MINE LODGED IN COURT
Traditional owners of the Jabiluka uranium deposit in the Northern Territory says the Federal Government will have to set the law straight if their court case against the mining project succeeds.
Representative Jacqui Katona says a statement of claims is being lodged in the Federal Court in Sydney today.
It challenges the right of the Northern Territory government to grant a mineral lease covering uranium.
Ms Katona says if the action is successful it will require legislative action under the Atomic Energy Act to allow permission to be granted for the mining of uranium.
NATIONAL CRIME AUTHORITY DEFENDED AT HEARING
The Victorian Bar Council says the National Crime Authority is more than a policing agency and shouldn't be absorbed by the Federal Police.
The Council's Susan Crennan has addressed the first day of Melbourne hearings by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on the NCA.
Ms Crennan says state police authorities can't possibly deal with their own responsibilities as well as fight national crime.
She says some people think the NCA's place could be taken by a strengthened Federal Police Force, but the NCA is not just a super police force.
She says it's a high level investigative national body.
GOVERNMENT TELL JUDGES TO KEEP OUT OF POLITICAL ARENA
The Federal Government says judges should keep out of the political arena.
Last week, the Chief Justice of the Family Court, Alistair Nicholson, criticised the Government's response to the Aboriginal stolen children inquiry, at an international conference on family law.
Acting Federal Attorney-General, Philip Ruddock, says the doctrine of the separation of powers -- which divides the Government and the judiciary -- is a two way street.

Mr Ruddock' has told ABC Radio judges should not be commenting on areas outside their portfolio responsibility that are in the public domain, because that compromises the separation of powers doctrine.
He says the Chief Justice should be conscious of the doctrine and the obligation of judges to keep out of the political arena.
KENNETT RULES OUT ROYAL COMMISSION INTO ALLEGED EXPERIMENTS
Victorian Premier, Jeff Kennett, says the laws of the day were followed if orphaned babies were used for medical experiments after World War Two.
The Federal Health Minister, Dr Michael Wooldridge, says the Victorian Government was ultimately responsible for the babies' care, and should now do what it can to track down the people affected.
And The Democrats want a Royal Commission.
But Mr Kennett has ruled out a Royal Commission saying even though present day education and standards may be different, nothing can change what happened 20 or 50 years ago.
He says this is 1997 and it's not possible to reinvent the past.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
